observations.note: This program feeds bencoder.encode() only ints, so line 1/3/4 can only ever contain the bytes 'l', 'i', 'e', '-', and ASCII digits '0'-'9'. A quote, backslash, or non-printable byte is unreachable. The rules below are inferred from CPython's PyBytes_Repr (Objects/bytesobject.c) and are marked INFERRED in implementation_rules items 14-19.

implementation_rules: Output is exactly four lines on stdout, in this fixed order: (1) repr of the bencoded list, (2) repr of the decoded list, (3) repr of the bencoded negation of a, (4) repr of the bencoded zero. Nothing else is ever written to stdout.
Line terminator is a single LF byte 0x0a. Never CRLF, never a bare CR. Verified: every probe had CR count = 0 and LF count = exactly 4.

A trailing LF IS present: the last byte of stdout is always 0x0a and there is no byte after it. In Node, write each of the four lines with process.stdout.write(line + "\n"), or equivalently console.log(line) four times.

On the success path stderr receives exactly 0 bytes and the exit code is 0. Confirmed by capturing 2>&1 and cmp'ing byte-for-byte against a stdout-only capture (IDENTICAL). Emit no warnings, no banners, no diagnostics.

The complete stdout for inputs a, b is the concatenation of: "b'li" + A + "ei" + B + "ei" + S + "ei" + P + "ee'
" + "[" + A + ", " + B + ", " + S + ", " + P + "]
" + "b'i" + N + "e'
" + "b'i0e'
", where A=str(a), B=str(b), S=str(a+b), P=str(a*b), N=str(-a). Validated byte-exactly over 105 (a,b) combinations plus the 4 documented cases.

Bytes-literal lines use prefix lowercase 'b' (0x62) immediately followed by the ASCII apostrophe 0x27 as the opening quote, the raw content bytes, then a closing 0x27. There is NO space between b and the quote and no space inside the quotes.

The list repr line uses '[' (0x5b) ... ']' (0x5d) with items separated by exactly comma-space, bytes 0x2c 0x20. There is no space after '[' , no space before ']', and no trailing comma (the list always has exactly 4 elements).

Integers are rendered as plain decimal with no thousands separators, no scientific notation, no '+' sign, and no leading zeros. Negative values get a single leading '-' (0x2d). Zero is always the single character '0' - there is no '-0' even when a==0 and the program computes -a (verified with --a 0 and --a -0).

Bencoded integer encoding is 'i' + decimal string + 'e'. The list encoding is 'l' + concatenation of the four encoded ints + 'e'. So line 1 always starts with the 4 bytes b'li and always ends with ee' before the newline.
Line 4 is the constant string b'i0e' for every input, unconditionally. Line 3 is b'i' + str(-a) + "e" - it is the negation of a only, never of b, and never of a+b.

Integers must be arbitrary precision. --a 99999999999999999999 --b 99999999999999999999 produced the exact 40-digit product 9999999999999999999800000000000000000001, and a 10**100 input produced exact 101-digit values with no rounding. In Node use BigInt for a, b, a+b, a*b, and -a; Number would silently corrupt these. Render with BigInt.prototype.toString() (which already matches Python's decimal formatting for all the cases above).
There is no line wrapping, truncation, ellipsis, or reflow for long values: a 10**100 input produced single lines of 317 / 312 / 107 characters plus their LFs (746 bytes total, still exactly 4 LF).

Output bytes are independent of environment and stream type: identical when stdout is a pipe vs a regular file, identical under LC_ALL=C/LANG=C, and identical under PYTHONIOENCODING=latin-1 and PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-16 (the frozen binary ignores it). Never emit a BOM. All output bytes are 7-bit ASCII, so UTF-8 and ASCII encodings coincide - write the buffer as 'utf8' or 'latin1' interchangeably.

INFERRED (unreachable in this program, implement for completeness): quote selection in a Python bytes repr. Scan the content bytes left to right; start with quote = single-quote. If a single-quote byte (0x27) is seen, switch quote to double-quote (0x22) and keep scanning; if a double-quote byte (0x22) is seen, set quote back to single-quote and stop scanning. Net effect: use " as the delimiter only when the content contains at least one ' and no " ; otherwise use ' .

INFERRED: inside the literal, the active quote character and the backslash byte 0x5c are each escaped with a preceding backslash. A quote byte that is NOT the active delimiter is emitted literally and unescaped - e.g. content b\x27\x22 chooses the single-quote delimiter and renders as b'\'\"'... more precisely: with delimiter ', a ' becomes \' and a " stays "; with delimiter ", a " cannot occur and a ' stays '.
INFERRED: only three control bytes get letter escapes: 0x09 -> \t, 0x0a -> \n, 0x0d -> \r. Notably 0x07 (bell) does NOT become \a and 0x0b/0x0c do NOT become \v/\f in Python's bytes repr.

INFERRED: any other byte c with c < 0x20 or c >= 0x7f (this includes 0x7f DEL and every byte 0x80-0xff) is rendered as \x followed by exactly two LOWERCASE hex digits, e.g. 0x00 -> \x00, 0x1b -> \x1b, 0xff -> \xff. No \u or \U forms are ever used for bytes.
INFERRED: every remaining byte in the printable ASCII range 0x20-0x7e (that is not the active delimiter and not backslash) is emitted verbatim, including the space character.
INFERRED: the b prefix is always present and always lowercase, even for empty content (repr of empty bytes is b'' - two quote characters with nothing between them).

For this specific program none of the inferred escape paths can trigger: bencoder.encode() on a list of Python ints yields only the bytes 'l' (0x6c), 'i' (0x69), 'e' (0x65), '-' (0x2d), and '0'-'9' (0x30-0x39), all printable ASCII and none equal to a quote or backslash. A reimplementation may therefore hardcode the single-quote delimiter with no escaping for these four lines and still be byte-exact.

implementation_rules: PROG NAME: prog = basename(process.argv[1]) as invoked (i.e. basename of the executable's argv[0]). For the shipped file this is exactly 'test14_executable'. It follows argv[0] verbatim: a renamed copy reports 'weird-name.bin', and `exec -a FAKEPROG` reports 'FAKEPROG'. Only the basename is used (no directory component). In Node, derive it from path.basename(process.argv[1]) (or process.argv[0] if reimplementing as a standalone binary).
USAGE STRING (single line at default width): `usage: <prog> [-h] --a A --b B` followed by LF. This exact line is the first line of --help (stdout) and the first line of every error report (stderr).

HELP OUTPUT (default width, i.e. COLUMNS unset/empty/non-numeric, or >= ~46): write exactly these 114 bytes to STDOUT and exit 0:
`usage: <prog> [-h] --a A --b B

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
  --b B
`
Details: one totally blank line (bare LF) between the usage line and `options:`; section header is `options:` (Python 3.10+ spelling, NOT `optional arguments:`); two-space indent before each entry; exactly two spaces between `-h, --help` and `show this help message and exit`; `--a A` and `--b B` have no help text and no trailing whitespace; file ends with LF.

HELP TRIGGERS: `-h`, `--help`, and any unambiguous long prefix of `--help` (`--h`, `--he`, `--hel`, `--hel`… anything that is a proper prefix of the string `--help`). Also `-h` bundled with junk (`-hx`, `-h5`, `-hh`) triggers help. Help always goes to stdout, prints once, and exits 0.

HELP PRECEDENCE (left-to-right scan): argparse processes tokens strictly left to right and executes the help action the moment it is reached. Therefore: (a) `-h` anywhere wins over missing-required-args and over unknown options regardless of position, because those two errors are only raised AFTER the whole scan finishes; (b) `-h` LOSES to an `invalid int value` or `expected one argument` error that occurs at an EARLIER token position, because those are raised during the scan. Implement as: scan tokens in order, raise value/arity errors immediately, but collect unknown tokens into an `extras` array and defer the required-args and unrecognized-args checks until after the scan.
EXIT CODES: 0 for a successful run and for help. 2 for every parse error. Nothing else observed.
STREAMS: help -> stdout. All parse errors -> stderr (both the usage block and the `prog: error: ...` line). On any parse error stdout is completely empty (the program body never runs).
ERROR FORMAT: emit the wrapped usage block, then `<prog>: error: <message>` then LF. The `prog: error:` line is NEVER wrapped, even at tiny COLUMNS.

ERROR MESSAGE CATALOGUE (exact strings):
1. `the following arguments are required: --a, --b` (or `--a` / `--b` alone) — names in declaration order, joined by `, `.
2. `argument --a: invalid int value: 'X'` / `argument --b: invalid int value: 'X'` — value single-quoted (Python repr of the str).
3. `argument --a: expected one argument` / `argument --b: expected one argument`.
4. `argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'` — note the action is named by ALL its option strings joined with `/`, not by what the user typed.
5. `unrecognized arguments: <extras joined by a single space>`.
6. `ambiguous option: <token> could match --help, --a, --b` — candidate list in declaration order joined with `, `.

ERROR PRECEDENCE (strict order): (1) errors raised during the left-to-right scan — `ignored explicit argument`, `ambiguous option`, `expected one argument`, `invalid int value` — fire at the first offending token and abort immediately; only the leftmost one is ever reported. (2) After the scan, if `-h`/`--help` was seen, print help and exit 0. (3) Otherwise, if any required option is missing -> `the following arguments are required: ...` and exit 2. (4) Otherwise, if `extras` is non-empty -> `unrecognized arguments: ...` and exit 2. Consequence: an unknown option is NEVER reported when a required option is also missing.

TOKEN CLASSIFICATION (does this token look like an option?): a token is a candidate option iff it is non-empty, starts with `-`, is not exactly `-`, is not exactly `--`, does NOT match the negative-number pattern `^-\d+$` or `^-\d*\.\d+$` (since no declared option looks like a negative number), and does NOT contain a space character. Everything else is a positional/value token. Verified: `-` , `-5`, `-1.5`, `+a`, `''`, `\t`, `--a 5` (one token with a space) are all classified as positionals.

LONG-OPTION MATCHING (allow_abbrev=True): split the token at the FIRST `=` into name and explicit value (only if `=` is present). Exact match on name wins. Otherwise collect every declared long option that STARTS WITH the name (the typed name must be a prefix of the declared option — `--ab` does NOT match `--a`). Zero matches -> unknown -> push the WHOLE ORIGINAL token (including any `=value`) into extras. Exactly one match -> use it. Two or more -> `ambiguous option: <original token> could match --help, --a, --b` (declaration order). Special case: `--` followed immediately by `=` gives an empty name, which is a prefix of all three long options -> ambiguous (`--=5`, `--=`).
CASE SENSITIVITY: option names are case sensitive. `--A`, `--B`, `--A=5`, `--B=5` are all unknown.

SINGLE-DASH FORMS: the only declared short option is `-h`. `-a`, `-b`, `-ab`, `-x`, `-z` are unknown -> extras. Bundling: for a token `-XYZ...` where `X` names a known ZERO-argument option, take that action then re-interpret `-` + rest; if the remainder is not a known short option, push `-` + remainder into extras. Because the only zero-arg option is `-h` (which exits), `-hANYTHING` always prints help and exits 0, while `-Xh` (unknown first char) is entirely unknown.

'=' VALUE FORM: `--a=5` == `--a 5`. Split on the FIRST `=` only: `--a=` -> value `''`; `--a==5` -> value `'=5'`; `--a=5=6` -> value `'5=6'`. Unlike the space form, the `=` form accepts option-looking values verbatim (`--a=-5`, `--a=--b`, `--a=-h`). Supplying `=value` to the zero-arg help option is an error (`ignored explicit argument`).

VALUE CONSUMPTION FOR --a/--b (nargs=None, exactly one value): if the token came with `=`, use that. Otherwise take the NEXT token, but only if it is not a candidate option and not `--`. `-5`/`-1.5`-style tokens ARE accepted as values. If the next token is a candidate option (`--b`, `-h`, `-x`) or is `--`, or there is no next token, raise `argument --X: expected one argument`.
REPEATED OPTIONS: plain store semantics — the LAST occurrence wins (`--a 5 --a 7` gives a=7). No error, no warning.

'--' SEPARATOR: the first `--` switches the rest of the command line to positional-only mode. Since the program declares NO positional arguments, everything after `--` (and the `--` token itself) ends up in extras verbatim. Consequences: `-- --a 5 --b 5` -> `required: --a, --b`; `--a 5 -- --b 5` -> `required: --b`; `--a 5 --b 5 --` -> `unrecognized arguments: --` (exit 2 despite otherwise-valid args); `--a 5 --b 5 -- x` -> `unrecognized arguments: -- x`; `--a 5 --b 5 -- -- x` -> `unrecognized arguments: -- -- x`. Do NOT strip `--` from extras.

EXTRAS ORDERING AND JOINING: extras preserve original argv order even when interleaved with recognized options (`--c 3 --a 5 --d --b 5 e` -> `--c 3 --d e`). Join with a single space and do not quote or escape: an empty-string extra produces a message ending in a trailing space; a tab or embedded newline is echoed raw (so the message can span multiple physical lines); UTF-8 bytes are passed through unchanged.

INTERSPERSED PARSING: options and stray positionals may be freely interleaved; options after a stray positional are still parsed normally (`--a 5 x --b 5` -> only `x` is unrecognized). Option order on the command line never affects the result — the output list is always [a, b, a+b, a*b].

USAGE/HELP WRAPPING (only needed for fidelity when COLUMNS is set): width = COLUMNS - 2 when COLUMNS parses as an integer, else 80 - 2 = 78 (non-tty stdout falls back to 80; empty or non-numeric COLUMNS also falls back). Usage wrapping: prefix `usage: ` (7 chars); if `usage: <prog> [-h] --a A --b B` fits in width, emit one line; else try putting the option group on continuation lines aligned under the first option (column 7 + len(prog) + 1); if prog itself plus one group does not fit, put prog alone on the first line and wrap the option parts with a 7-space indent. Help-entry layout: help_column = min(14, min(24, max(width - 20, 4))) where 14 = len('  -h, --help') + 2; if len('-h, --help') <= help_column - 4 the help text starts on the same line at help_column, otherwise `  -h, --help` gets its own line and the help text is written on following lines indented by help_column; help text is word-wrapped to max(width - help_column, 11) columns. `  --a A` and `  --b B` never wrap.

A from-scratch Node implementation only needs the default-width layout to match all realistic invocations; hardcoding the 114-byte help block and the single-line usage string is sufficient unless COLUMNS fidelity is required.

implementation_rules: Use BigInt for all arithmetic. Parse --a and --b into BigInt, compute sum = a + b and product = a * b with BigInt, and render with BigInt.prototype.toString() (base 10). Never route any value through Number/parseInt/parseFloat — 2**53 vs 2**53+1 and (2**53)**2 vs (2**53+1)**2 are observably distinct in the output.

Output is always exactly 4 lines, in this order: (1) the bencoded list, (2) the decoded list repr, (3) the bencoding of -a, (4) the literal b'i0e'. stdout ends with exactly one \n (0x0A) after line 4 and contains no \r, no BOM, and no trailing blank line.
Line 1 format: `b'l` + INT(a) + INT(b) + INT(a+b) + INT(a*b) + `e'` where INT(x) = 'i' + x.toString() + 'e'. Concatenated with no separators. Example for a=5,b=5: b'li5ei5ei10ei25ee'
Line 2 format: `[` + [a, b, a+b, a*b].map(String).join(', ') + `]`. The separator is a comma followed by exactly one space. No brackets-per-element, no quotes, no BigInt 'n' suffix.
Line 3 format: `b'i` + (-a).toString() + `e'`. Line 4 is the constant string `b'i0e'` regardless of inputs.

Negative zero must never appear. When a === 0n, -a is 0n and line 3 must be b'i0e', never b'i-0e'. Likewise a+b === 0n renders as `i0e` inside line 1 and as `0` inside line 2. Inputs '-0', '000', '-000' all normalise to 0.

Sign rendering: negative values get a single leading '-' immediately after the 'i' (e.g. i-100e) and immediately inside the list (e.g. [-100, ...]). Positive values never carry a '+'. No zero padding, no grouping, no exponent notation, no truncation — ever, at any magnitude.

Input parsing must replicate Python int(str): optional surrounding ASCII whitespace (space, \t, \n, \r, \f, \v) is stripped; an optional single leading '+' or '-' is allowed; underscores are allowed between digits and are removed; leading zeros are allowed and stripped. Base-10 digits only — reject '1e30', '0x...', '1.0', empty/whitespace-only.

Enforce Python 3.12's sys.int_max_str_digits = 4300 on PARSING: if the input's decimal digit count (after removing underscores, sign, and whitespace, and NOT counting leading zeros' effect on the parsed value — measured on the digit characters supplied) exceeds 4300, argparse rejects it. Emit to stderr `usage: test14_executable [-h] --a A --b B\ntest14_executable: error: argument --<name>: invalid int value: '<the full original argument verbatim>'\n`, write nothing to stdout, and exit with code 2. The argument is echoed in full, never truncated (a 5000-char arg produces a ~5100-byte stderr).
Underscores do not count toward the 4300 limit: a 5374-character argument containing 4300 digits plus separators parses successfully.

Enforce the same 4300-digit limit on OUTPUT (int -> str conversion) for every one of the four list elements. Since |a| and |b| are already <= 4300 digits after parsing, only a+b and a*b can overflow. If the decimal-digit count of |a+b| or |a*b| exceeds 4300, the program must print NOTHING to stdout (the failure occurs while building line 1, before any print) and write this to stderr, then exit with code 1:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test14.py", line 10, in <module>
  File "bencoder.py", line 41, in encode
  File "bencoder.py", line 35, in encode
ValueError: Exceeds the limit (4300 digits) for integer string conversion; use sys.set_int_max_str_digits() to increase the limit
[PYI-<pid>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test14' due to unhandled exception!

The <pid> in the [PYI-...] line is the running process id (use process.pid). It changes on every run and must not be hard-coded. The stderr block is 367 bytes when the pid is 4 digits and ends with a single \n.

The digit-limit threshold is strict: exactly 4300 digits succeeds, 4301 fails. Verified at the boundary — a=10**2149 (2150 digits) times b=10**2150 (2151 digits) gives a 4300-digit product and exits 0; b=10**2151 gives a 4301-digit product and exits 1. The '-' sign does not count as a digit (a 4300-digit negative renders as a 4306-character line 3).
The digit-count check applies to the magnitude only; compute it as (x < 0n ? -x : x).toString().length, or equivalently guard before stringifying if you want to avoid materialising oversized strings.

The bytes object repr always uses single quotes (b'...') because the payload contains only digits and the characters l, i, e, and '-' — no quote characters can ever appear, so the double-quote repr form is unreachable.
Exit codes: 0 on success; 2 for argparse int-parse failure (including the >4300-digit input rejection); 1 for the encode-time ValueError when a sum or product exceeds 4300 digits.
